sanskrit:
धृतराष्ट्र उवाच ।
धर्मक्षेत्रे कुरुक्षेत्रे समवेता युयुत्सवः ।
मामकाः पाण्डवाश्चैव किमकुर्वत सञ्जय ॥
translation: Dhritarashtra said: What did the sons of Pandu and my own sons do, O Sanjaya, when they assembled, eager to fight, on the sacred field of Kurukshetra?
explanation: The Gita opens with a blind king's anxious question. Dhritarashtra's own words betray him — he separates "my sons" from "Pandu's sons," revealing the attachment and partiality that will drive the entire tragedy. The battlefield is called dharma-kshetra, the field of righteousness, hinting that this is more than a war — it is a test of conscience.

sanskrit:
कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन ।
मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि ॥
translation: You have a right to perform your duty, but never to the fruits of your actions. Let not the fruit of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction.
explanation: Perhaps the most quoted verse in the Gita. Krishna teaches Karma Yoga — act fully, with sincerity and skill, but release the anxious grip on results. This isn't a call to apathy; it's a call to freedom from the exhausting cycle of hope and fear that comes from chasing outcomes.

sanskrit:
न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचिंन्नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः ।
अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो
न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे ॥
translation: The soul is never born, nor does it ever die. It has not come into being, nor will it cease to be. It is unborn, eternal, permanent, and primeval. It is not slain when the body is slain.
explanation: Krishna consoles Arjuna with the core metaphysics of the Gita: the true self (Atman) is not the body. Bodies are temporary garments; the soul that wears them is untouched by birth or death. Grief over the body's fate, Krishna suggests, is grief over a shadow.

sanskrit:
वासांसि जीर्णानि यथा विहाय
नवानि गृह्णाति नरोऽपराणि ।
तथा शरीराणि विहाय जीर्णा
न्यन्यानि संयाति नवानि देही ॥
translation: As a person casts off worn-out garments and puts on new ones, so the soul casts off worn-out bodies and enters into others that are new.
explanation: One of the Gita's most vivid images. Death is reframed not as an ending but as a change of clothing — the wearer (the soul) continues on. This verse is often cited as a foundation for the Hindu understanding of reincarnation.

sanskrit:
यदा यदा हि धर्मस्य ग्लानिर्भवति भारत ।
अभ्युत्थानमधर्मस्य तदात्मानं सृजाम्यहम् ॥
translation: Whenever righteousness declines and unrighteousness rises, O Arjuna, I manifest Myself on earth.
explanation: Krishna reveals the doctrine of divine descent (avatara). Whenever moral order collapses, the divine takes form to restore balance — not as a one-time event, but as a recurring pattern through the ages.

sanskrit:
उद्धरेदात्मनाऽऽत्मानं नात्मानमवसादयेत् ।
आत्मैव ह्यात्मनो बन्धुरात्मैव रिपुरात्मनः ॥
translation: Let a person lift themselves by their own self; let them not degrade themselves. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.
explanation: A quietly radical verse: your greatest ally and your greatest obstacle are both within you. Krishna places the responsibility for growth squarely on the individual — no one else can lift you, and no one else can hold you down, unless you let them.

sanskrit:
सर्वधर्मान्परित्यज्य मामेकं शरणं व्रज ।
अहं त्वा सर्वपापेभ्यो मोक्षयिष्यामि मा शुचः ॥
translation: Abandon all varieties of dharma and simply surrender unto Me alone. I shall liberate you from all sinful reactions; do not fear.
explanation: Often called the charama-shloka, the Gita's final teaching. After 700 verses of philosophy, action, and meditation, Krishna's ultimate instruction is startlingly simple: surrender. This verse anchors the entire path of Bhakti Yoga, devotion as the direct route to liberation.
